analysis.headline: Alberta and the oil price change

blocks.text: For an oil-price change of -10%, Canada's nominal GDP changes by -0.5% in the first year after the shock and -0.6% in the second. Real GDP changes by -0.1% and -0.1%, respectively. This is a national persistent oil-price sensitivity on Finance Canada's 2026 baseline. It uses a local linear approximation of the published illustration. It cannot be allocated to provinces or added to CER scenario results.
Alberta accounted for 57.43% of Canada's energy-sector value added in 2022. This is a share of the energy sector, not of Canada's total GDP or federal revenue.

In 2022, Alberta's energy sector generated 163,605.9 million current CAD in value added, or 35.84% of its GDP at basic prices. This measures where production occurs, not where owners live or how the income is distributed.

These sources do not provide provincial GDP, jobs, royalty or household-bill responses to arbitrary commodity-price changes. The CER cases compare complete scenarios, and the oil-price sensitivity is national only.

limitations: GDP records value added where production occurs. It does not identify the residence of owners or everyone who benefits.
The national GDP comparison is the sum of 13 provinces and territories at basic prices. It is not expenditure GDP at market prices.
CER scenarios change several assumptions together. Their differences are not the causal effect of changing one price.
Delivered residential price indices compare scenarios in the same year. The source price basis requires reconciliation, so dollar bills are not estimated.
No calibrated provincial GDP, employment, royalty or household-income response to arbitrary commodity prices is included.
Oil sensitivity is a separate national Finance Canada illustration on its 2026 baseline. Do not add it to CER scenario changes or allocate it to provinces.
Missing source combinations remain unavailable. They do not establish zero production or zero cost.
Provincial GDP, jobs and household bill responses to arbitrary price changes are not estimated.

Quebec accounted for 6.41% of Canada's energy-sector value added in 2022. This is a share of the energy sector, not of Canada's total GDP or federal revenue.

Provincial GDP records where value is added; it does not identify everyone who receives the income. Household energy costs and the distribution of benefits within a province require separate measures.
